title: Lesson 19: Change Management and Adoption: Getting Real People to Actually Use the System
description: Getting real people to adopt a delivered system by separating change from adoption, treating resistance as information, designing the agent into the way people already work, and measuring success in usage rather than shipped features.

questions.question: What is the difference between change and adoption?
options: Change is what the client pays for; adoption is what the consultant delivers
Change is how the system works; adoption is how people behave in using it
Change is a technical task; adoption is a training session
Change is measured in features; adoption is measured in meetings held
questions.explanation: Shipping the technical change and changing people's behavior are separate outcomes; a system nobody uses is change without adoption, which is a cost rather than value.

questions.question: What does user resistance usually indicate?
options: That the users lack sufficient training on the new system
That the manager has not mandated the tool strongly enough
That a concern about fit or trust was not answered
That the tool needs more features before people will try it
questions.explanation: Resistance is information: it points to an unanswered question about whether the change fits the user's work or can be trusted.

questions.question: Which arrangement best supports adoption sticking?
options: An owner who removes obstacles plus a champion with the pain
A senior sponsor who mandates the tool by memo to the whole team
A company-wide training program delivered to every affected user
A feature-rich release announced before anyone has used the tool
questions.explanation: Authority unblocks a tool while credibility spreads it, so adoption needs both the owner and a champion with real skin in the game.
